title: Preble: Efficient Distributed Prompt Scheduling for LLM Serving
technique: Distributed prefix-aware scheduling: E2 (exploration+exploitation) global scheduler co-optimizing KV prefix reuse and load balance, with autoscaling of hot prefixes, prefill/decode-aware mixing, and fairness-aware local priority queue

optimized_metrics.evidence: Preble ... aims to provide high serving throughput and low request average and tail latency for long and shared prompts.
optimized_metrics.stat_quote: low request average and tail latency

optimized_metrics.evidence: We consider p99 latency since it is important to control the tail latency in LLM serving as with all other user-facing services
optimized_metrics.stat_quote: We consider p99 latency since it is important to control the tail latency

optimized_metrics.evidence: Preble aims to provide high serving throughput and low request average and tail latency for long and shared prompts.
Preble aims to achieve high prefix reusing while ensuring fairness, which is important in multi-tenancy environments.
a naive solution that always sends requests with shared prefixes to the same GPU would result in imbalanced loads and low overall GPU utilization

headline_claim.text: Preble outperforms the SOTA serving systems by 1.5× to 14.5× on average latency and 2× to 10× on p99 latency.

reported_metrics.where: RPS sustained at given latency; global scheduler max throughput §4.5

metric_definitions.definition_quote: We use three key metrics: request per second, which measures serving capacity; average end-to-end request latency (including scheduling time, queueing time, prefill, and decoding time); and p99 request latency.
metric_definitions.notes: E2E includes scheduling and queueing; RPS = serving capacity

metric_definitions.definition_quote: Note that our metrics differ slightly from some existing LLM serving works Kwon et al. (2023); Yu et al. (2022), as we do not use TPOT (time per output token) or TTFT (time to first token) as key metrics. This is because our target LLM use has short output lengths, rendering TPOT not as meaningful and TTFT close to the request latency.
metric_definitions.notes: explicit justification for E2E over TTFT/TPOT; TTFT and TPOT only shown in Fig 4 on Azure trace

load_regime: request-rate sweep (Poisson arrivals, RPS on x-axis) plus Azure trace arrival pattern for tool-use/video-QA mix
tradeoff_acknowledged: Local fairness-oriented priority wait queue improves p99 but not average latency (ablation)
hardware: two-server cluster, each with two NVIDIA A6000 GPUs; one eight-H100 server
workloads: five long/shared-prompt workloads (toolbench tool use, VideoQA, programming, long document QA, etc.); Azure LLM trace arrival pattern
extractor_notes: Notable: paper deliberately avoids TTFT/TPOT, uses E2E mean and p99 plus RPS capacity. Text says 'A600' in one place (typo for A6000). The scheduler's internal cost is in GPU-computation-time units ('prompt-aware load').
